title: Bicycles and Traffic Rules: The Rules Students Break First
summary: A bicycle in Japan is a vehicle in law. Drink-riding one carries up to 5 years. Most students learn this from a police officer rather than in advance.
body_html:
A bicycle is the first thing most students buy and the first law most of them break. Not out of recklessness — out of a reasonable assumption that a bicycle is a bicycle.

In Japan it is a vehicle, and the penalties follow from that.

Start with the penalties, because they are the surprise

These are the penalties for bicycle offences, not car offences.

Drink-riding in the drunk-riding category carries imprisonment of up to 5 years or a fine of up to 1,000,000 yen. [source:3] The alcohol-present category carries up to 3 years or up to 500,000 yen, and the threshold is a breath alcohol concentration of 0.15 mg or more per 1 litre. [source:3]

Read that again with the vehicle in mind. Riding home from a drinking party is in the same category of offence as driving home from one.

Using a phone and thereby causing an accident or creating a traffic danger carries up to 1 year or up to 300,000 yen. [source:3] Merely holding a phone to talk or to look at the screen carries up to 6 months or up to 100,000 yen. [source:3]

Failing to assist after causing an accident carries up to 1 year or up to 100,000 yen; failing to report one carries up to 3 months or up to 50,000 yen. [source:3] The guidebook notes these are not an exhaustive list — other violations carry penalties too. [source:3]

The five rules, and the one that trips everyone

The rules are published as the five rules for safe bicycle use. [source:2]

Rule 1: the roadway is the principle, ride on the left. [source:2] The pavement is the exception, pedestrians have priority. [source:2] A bicycle is a vehicle and as a rule keeps to the left side of the roadway. [source:2] Where there is a cycle track, use the cycle track. [source:2] You may ride in the roadside band on the left side of the road, but must not obstruct pedestrians. [source:2]

This is the one. Riding on the right feels harmless and is wrong, and riding on the pavement is not a general right.

The pavement is permitted where a sign indicates pavement riding is allowed. [source:2] Separately, children under 13 years of age, elderly people aged 70 and over, and people with physical disabilities may ride on the pavement. [source:1] When riding on the pavement you must proceed slowly near the roadway side at a speed that allows you to stop immediately, and you must stop temporarily where there is a risk of obstructing pedestrians. [source:1]

Rule 2: at intersections, obey signals and stop signs, and check it is safe. [source:1] Where there is a signal, proceed after it turns green and after checking it is safe. [source:1] Where an intersection requires a temporary stop, always stop. [source:1]

Rule 3: use your light at night. [source:1] You must turn your light on at night, and the guidebook suggests checking it works before you set off. [source:1]

Rule 4: no drink-riding. [source:1] If you have been drinking, never ride a bicycle. [source:1]

Rule 5: wear a helmet. [source:1] The guidebook asks you to wear a cycling helmet, and to wear it correctly by fastening the chin strap securely. [source:1]

The other rules, including one that costs money

You must not use a smartphone or mobile phone while riding. [source:3] Riding two to a bicycle and riding side by side are both to be avoided. [source:3] You must not ride while holding an umbrella, or while using earphones in a state where you cannot adequately hear your surroundings. [source:3] Bicycles are prohibited from entering expressways. [source:3]

Then the one almost nobody mentions.

Bicycle liability insurance is compulsory in many areas. Insurance can cover compensation to victims of a bicycle accident and your own injuries, and the guidebook states that bicycle liability compensation insurance in particular must be taken out in many regions, including Tokyo and Osaka. [source:3]

Must, not should. If you are in Tokyo and riding an uninsured bicycle, you are not merely taking a risk — you are out of compliance with the local requirement. Some school dormitories and some bicycle shops bundle this; many do not. Ask, in your first week.

The electric bicycle trap

This distinction decides whether you need a licence, and the machines look similar.

A power-assisted bicycle carrying the TS mark counts as a bicycle and may be ridden without a licence. [source:3] But a vehicle that merely resembles a bicycle, if it is self-propelled or exceeds the assist-ratio standard, counts as a pedal-equipped electric motorbike — which requires a licence, compulsory vehicle liability insurance, and a number plate. [source:3]

So "electric bike" is not one category. Buying the wrong one and riding it unlicensed is unlicensed riding, whatever the shop told you.

Electric kick scooters are a third category

These are specified small motorised bicycles, and the type includes bicycle-shaped and seated models, not only the kick-scooter shape. [source:4]

No licence is needed to ride one, but riding by a person under 16 years of age is prohibited. [source:4] If the vehicle does not meet the size and structure standards it becomes a vehicle requiring a licence. [source:4] A number plate and compulsory vehicle liability insurance are required. [source:4]

You must ride on the roadway. [source:4] Pavement riding is limited to a mode restricted to a maximum speed of 6 km/h, and only where a road sign indicates pavement riding is permitted. [source:4] You must keep to the left edge and must not ride on the right side. [source:4] Drink-riding is absolutely prohibited, as is lending one to someone who has been drinking. [source:4] Riding two-up and side by side are prohibited, as is using an umbrella or a phone while riding. [source:4] Expressways are prohibited, and the guidebook asks you to wear a helmet. [source:4]

Walking, briefly — it has rules too

Use the pavement or the roadside band where there is one; on roads without either, walk on the right edge. [source:1] You cannot walk on an expressway. [source:1]

Cross at a pedestrian crossing or a signalised intersection where one is nearby, and use a footbridge or underpass where one is nearby. [source:1] Where a no-pedestrian-crossing sign is posted, do not cross. [source:1] Crossing diagonally is not allowed, and the guidebook suggests raising your hand to signal your intention to drivers. [source:1]

At a railway crossing, always stop before it and check both directions. [source:1] Do not enter once the alarm is sounding or the barrier has begun to descend. [source:1] Some crossings have neither alarm nor barrier — stop before those too. [source:1]

And one piece of advice worth taking literally: when walking at night, wear bright clothing and attach reflective items to your shoes, clothes, bag or cane so drivers can see you. [source:1]

If you want to drive

There are three ways to drive a car or motorbike in Japan: obtaining a Japanese licence, driving on an international driving permit issued by a party to the Geneva Convention in the prescribed form, or driving on a foreign licence accompanied by an embassy-prepared Japanese translation — the last available for 6 countries and regions. [source:5]

The second and third routes allow driving for at most 1 year. [source:5] That limit is the part students miss: an international permit is not a long-term solution for a two-year stay.

To convert a foreign licence, you must have stayed in the issuing country for 3 months or more after obtaining it, and if your knowledge and skills are confirmed as adequate the written and practical tests are waived. [source:5]

The short version

  • Ride on the left, on the roadway. The pavement needs a sign. [source:2]
  • Lights at night, helmet on, no phone in your hand. [source:1] [source:3]
  • Never ride after drinking. It is up to 5 years. [source:3]
  • Check whether your prefecture requires bicycle liability insurance, and get it. Tokyo and Osaka do. [source:3]
  • Before buying anything electric, ask whether it carries the TS mark or needs a licence. [source:3]
  • If you plan to drive, plan for a Japanese licence — the permit routes run out. [source:5]

Related: the rest of the guidebook and how to get the current edition, in the official guidebook; what to do when an accident or emergency happens, in emergency numbers; and the rubbish and noise rules, including what it costs to dispose of a bicycle when you leave, in daily-life rules.

All of the above is from the transport chapter of the guidebook, cited by page range below. Local requirements vary by prefecture — yours is the authority on its own insurance rule.

claims_without_sources: 「自転車は留学生が最初に破る法規である」—— 当方の観察であり、違反統計に基づくものではない。
「右側通行は無害に感じる」—— 読者の心理についての推測。
「学校の寮や自転車店が保険を扱っている場合もあるが、扱っていないことも多い」—— 当方の経験に基づく記述で、冊子には書かれていない。だから「一週目に聞け」という助言の形にした。
「店が何と言ったかに関わらず無免許運転になる」—— 条文の適用についての当方の読み。冊子は免許が必要であると述べているのみ。
「国際免許は二年の滞在には足りない」—— 冊子の「長くて1年」という記述からの帰結であって、冊子がこの結論を書いているわけではない。
都道府県ごとの自転車保険条例の一覧 —— 冊子は「東京都や大阪府など、多くの地域」と書くのみで、網羅的な一覧を示していない。したがって本文も網羅を主張せず、自分の自治体に確認せよと書いた。
本記事は同一の PDF を5つの出典として、章内の節ごとにページ範囲を分けて引いている。第9章全体（約1万字）を1つの出典にすると、自動車の罰則表と自転車の罰則表が同じ干し草の山に入り、金額を書き換えても闸门が黙ることを変異テストで確認したため。
